text:
Help me write a case for my promotion. I'm the assistant front office manager at a 180-room hotel, and the front office manager job is open. I'm applying, and my general manager wants it in writing by Friday.

Facts:
- I've worked here 6 years, the last 2 as assistant manager.
- Our guest score for check-in on the main review site went from 7.9 to 8.6 over the last 18 months. The lobby and all the rooms were renovated during the same time.
- I rewrote the front desk training. New hires now work the desk alone after 5 shifts instead of 9.
- Front desk turnover was 9 of 14 people in the year before I became assistant manager, and 5 of 14 last year.
- I've covered the front office manager's job alone for the 7 weeks since she left.
- I have never managed a budget. The front office manager owns a $1.1 million payroll budget.

I want it to say I'm the main reason our guest scores went up. One page.

Before I draft, there's one problem with the claim you want to make, and I have a few questions.

## The problem with "I'm the main reason scores went up"

- **What you want to say:** you're the main reason the check-in score went from 7.9 to 8.6.
- **What your facts support:** the score rose during your time running the desk, but the lobby and every room were renovated over the same 18 months.

Your GM approved that renovation and knows exactly when it happened. A new lobby can raise a check-in score all by itself. If you claim the credit outright, your GM is likely to think of the renovation straight away, and it will make them doubt the rest of the page too.

**A version your facts support now:** the score went up while you were running the desk, and you changed the things a check-in score measures. Training was rewritten, new hires work alone after 5 shifts instead of 9, and turnover fell from 9 of 14 people (64%) to 5 of 14 (36%). A renovated lobby doesn't make a check-in faster. Experienced, well-trained staff do.

**What could let you make the stronger claim:** evidence that separates your work from the renovation (question 1 below). If you have it, the page can say more.

It's your call. My recommendation is the narrower version unless you have that evidence.

## How the argument is built

- **What we want the GM to agree to:** you should be the front office manager.
- **Facts the GM will accept on sight:** 6 years at the hotel, 2 as assistant manager. Training cut from 9 shifts to 5. Turnover down from 64% to 36%. Check-in score up from 7.9 to 8.6. 7 weeks doing the job alone.
- **The idea linking those facts to the promotion:** the best predictor of how someone will do a job is how they've already done it. You've done this one for 7 weeks, and you built the team.
- **What could sink it:** you've never managed a budget, and this job owns a $1.1M payroll. The renovation weakens your claim on the score. The GM might also want an outside hire with budget experience.

The budget is the objection your GM will raise first, so the page has to answer it, not hide it.

## Questions

1. **Can you separate your work from the renovation?** For example: did the check-in score start rising before the renovation finished? Do reviews mention front desk staff by name or praise the check-in itself? Did the check-in score rise more than scores for things like rooms or cleanliness?
2. **What have you done that touches payroll, even without owning the budget?** Building schedules, controlling overtime, approving hours, staffing to occupancy. What did that look like over these 7 weeks? Would you commit to something specific, like a finance course or monthly reviews with the GM or controller in your first quarter? I'll only include it if you'll stand behind it.
3. **What specifically happened in the 7 weeks?** Anything the GM saw or heard about: a busy period, a problem you handled, scores holding steady or improving.
4. **What did you do about turnover?** Was the training rewrite the main change, or did you also change hiring, scheduling or something else? When did the new training start?
5. **Is there anything the GM has against you, or are there other candidates?** For example, an external candidate with budget experience.
6. **How should the page be addressed and signed?** I'll need the GM's name and how you want it signed. Should it be a letter or a memo?

Answer what you can. Anything you don't know, I'll leave out rather than guess.

1. Some. The renovation didn't start until 5 months into the 18 months, and check-in had already gone from 7.9 to 8.2 by then. I don't know about reviews naming staff or how check-in compares to the room or cleanliness scores. I'm fine with saying what I did instead of "main reason."

2. In the 7 weeks, no front desk shift went uncovered and overtime came in under the monthly plan. I'll commit to finishing the company's finance course in my first 3 months (the company pays for it). I'll also do weekly sessions on the payroll budget with our controller, Ben Oduya. He's already offered.

3. Same as above: every shift covered, overtime under plan. Nothing else specific I can point to.

4. I don't know beyond the training rewrite. I don't have the exact start date.

5. There's an outside candidate. I can't match their experience at a bigger hotel. Also, Friday evening check-in waits are still our most common complaint at the desk, so that could come up.

6. To Mark Ellison, the GM. Signed Daniela Ruiz. Letter or memo, whichever you think is better.

Your answer to question 1 makes the score point stronger than I expected. Of the 0.7-point rise, 0.3 points came before renovation work started. I've built the score paragraph around that and kept your wording: it says what you did, not that you were the main reason.

<final_document>
**MEMO**

**To:** Mark Ellison, General Manager
**From:** Daniela Ruiz, Assistant Front Office Manager
**Re:** Application for Front Office Manager

I'm applying for the front office manager position. For the past 7 weeks I've done the job on my own, and I would like to keep doing it.

**The last 7 weeks**

Since the position opened, every front desk shift has been covered, and overtime has come in under the monthly plan each month. You don't have to guess how I would run the front office, because you've already seen me do it.

**My 2 years as assistant manager**

- **Training.** I rewrote the front desk training. New hires now work the desk alone after 5 shifts instead of 9, which is almost half the time it used to take.
- **Turnover.** In the year before I became assistant manager, the front desk lost 9 of its 14 people. Last year it lost 5.
- **Guest scores.** Over the last 18 months our check-in score on our main review site rose from 7.9 to 8.6. The renovation helped. But the score had already reached 8.2 before renovation work began, 5 months into that period, so almost half the gain came before anything in the lobby changed.

**The budget**

I've never managed a budget, and this role owns a $1.1 million payroll. Keeping overtime under plan for 7 weeks is my only payroll record, and it's a short one. To close that gap, I'll finish the company's finance course within my first 3 months. I'll also meet weekly with Ben Oduya to go through the payroll budget. He has already offered to do this.

**The outside candidate**

I know you're considering an outside candidate who has worked at a bigger hotel. I can't match that experience. What I can offer is 6 years at this hotel, a front desk team I trained, and 7 weeks already in this job. An outside hire would spend their first months learning this building and this team. I can start on the hotel's problems right away.

**What I'd fix first**

Friday evening check-in waits are still the most common complaint at our front desk. That's the first problem I would take on as front office manager.

I'd welcome the chance to talk this through with you before you decide.

Daniela Ruiz
</final_document>

Some things to check before you send it:

- **I went with a memo.** It's an internal decision with a deadline, and a memo's headings make it quick for Mark to scan. There's no date line, because you didn't give me one. Add it when you send.
- **Friday waits.** All the memo says is that this would be your first priority. If you have an actual fix in mind, like changing staffing on Friday evenings, add one sentence about it. That would make this section much stronger. I left it out because the idea needs to come from you.
- **Turnover.** The memo puts the turnover drop next to the training rewrite but doesn't say the training caused it, because you couldn't confirm that. If you find out when the new training started, and it was before turnover fell, you could connect the two.
- **"Each month."** I wrote that overtime came in under plan each month. If it was only under plan across the 7 weeks as a whole, delete "each month."
- **Review site.** If Mark would expect the site to be named, replace "our main review site" with its name.
